# Model 7  

# Modeling the story itself: how a false claim travelled

## The claim in the article

The article's own framing is that scary media reports circulated, and that even when people working on the ground tried to explain that buying quinoa was helping Andean farmers, what they had was anecdote rather than evidence. The evidence arrived years later, in working papers using ten years of ENAHO data.

For a course in *computational social science*, this is the most interesting model in the notebook — because the object being modeled is the discourse, not the market.

## The idea

A claim spreading through a population behaves much like an infection. At any moment, divide people into three groups:

- **S** — has not encountered the claim yet
- **B** — encountered it, believes it, repeats it to others
- **R** — has stopped repeating it, whether from boredom or from having seen the correction

The flows between them:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{new believers} &= \beta \, S \, B \quad \text{(a believer meets a susceptible)} \\
\text{people who drop it} &= \delta \, B
\end{aligned}
$$

The product $S \times B$ is the crucial term. It says transmission needs *both* someone to spread and someone to spread to — the same structure as the logistic in Models 3 and 4, now doing a third job. If you have followed this notebook you have now seen one mathematical form model an idea spreading, a herd of llamas hitting a limit, and a rumour propagating. That transferability is not a coincidence and it is not a trick; it is the reason formal modeling earns its keep across fields that share no subject matter.

## The question worth asking

The article's implicit criticism is about *timing*: the claim ran unopposed for years before anyone checked. So we run the same epidemic twice, changing only when the correction arrives, and ask what the correction buys.

```{r model7-contagion, fig.width=12.5, fig.height=5.1, out.width="100%"}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# MODEL 7: the spread of a claim, and the arrival of evidence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

MONTHS <- 72                # six years, roughly 2010 to 2016
STEP   <- 0.25              # we advance in quarter-month steps for smoothness

TRANSMISSION    <- 0.42     # "beta":  how readily the claim passes on
FORGETTING      <- 0.05     # "delta": how fast people drop it unprompted
EVIDENCE_EFFECT <- 8.0      # how much faster people drop it once evidence lands
SEED_SHARE      <- 0.002    # the tiny fraction who believe it at the very start

run_epidemic <- function(evidence_month) {
  # Three compartments, as fractions of the population, adding to 1.
  S <- 1.0 - SEED_SHARE
  B <- SEED_SHARE
  R <- 0.0

  # How many steps we will take, and empty rows of numbers to record each one.
  n_steps <- floor(MONTHS / STEP)
  out <- data.frame(t = numeric(n_steps), S = numeric(n_steps),
                    B = numeric(n_steps), R = numeric(n_steps))
  t <- 0.0

  for (i in seq_len(n_steps)) {
    # Has the debunking evidence been published yet? If so, people abandon
    # the claim much faster. Note we model evidence as changing a RATE, not
    # as instantly convincing everyone - which is the realistic version.
    drop_rate <- FORGETTING
    if (t >= evidence_month) {
      drop_rate <- FORGETTING * EVIDENCE_EFFECT
    }

    # The flows during this small slice of time.
    newly_convinced <- TRANSMISSION * S * B * STEP
    newly_dropped   <- drop_rate * B * STEP

    # Move people between compartments. Whatever leaves S enters B, and
    # whatever leaves B enters R. Nobody is created or destroyed - a useful
    # thing to check in any model of this kind.
    S <- S - newly_convinced
    B <- B + newly_convinced - newly_dropped
    R <- R + newly_dropped

    out[i, ] <- c(t, S, B, R)
    t <- t + STEP
  }

  out
}

# Two worlds: evidence at 12 months, and evidence at 42 months.
early <- run_epidemic(evidence_month = 12)
late  <- run_epidemic(evidence_month = 42)

# A helper of our own for drawing stacked bands. Base R has no stackplot, so we
# draw each band as a filled polygon: along the bottom edge left-to-right, then
# back along the top edge right-to-left. rev() reverses a row of numbers.
stacked_band <- function(t, lower, upper, colour) {
  polygon(c(t, rev(t)), c(lower, rev(upper)), col = colour, border = NA)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 5, 3.5, 1.5), oma = c(0, 0, 2.5, 0))

runs   <- list(early, late)
whens  <- c(12, 42)
titles <- c("Evidence published early (month 12)", "Evidence published late (month 42)")

for (k in 1:2) {
  run <- runs[[k]]
  t <- run$t
  # The three cumulative boundaries between the bands, in percentage points.
  b1 <- 100 * run$S                      # top of the "never heard it" band
  b2 <- 100 * (run$S + run$B)            # top of the "believes it" band

  y_label <- if (k == 1) "% of population" else ""

  plot(range(t), c(0, 100), type = "n", xlab = "months", ylab = y_label,
       main = titles[k], cex.main = 0.95)
  stacked_band(t, rep(0, length(t)), b1, TAB["pale"])    # never heard it
  stacked_band(t, b1, b2, TAB["red"])                    # believes and repeats it
  stacked_band(t, b2, rep(100, length(t)), TAB["steel"]) # no longer repeats it

  abline(v = whens[k], lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(whens[k] + 1, 88, "evidence\narrives", cex = 0.8, adj = 0)

  if (k == 1) {
    legend("left", legend = c("never heard it", "believes and repeats it",
                              "no longer repeats it"),
           fill = c(TAB["pale"], TAB["red"], TAB["steel"]),
           border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
  }
}

mtext("Model 7: the same claim, corrected early and corrected late",
      outer = TRUE, cex = 1.0)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0))

# How many people ever believed it? That is everyone who left S: 1 minus the
# fraction still in S at the end.
for (k in 1:2) {
  run  <- runs[[k]]
  name <- c("early correction", "late correction")[k]
  ever <- 100 * (1 - run$S[nrow(run)])
  peak <- 100 * max(run$B)
  peak_month <- run$t[which.max(run$B)]
  cat(sprintf("%-18s: %5.1f%% ever believed it | peak %4.1f%% believing at once, in month %.0f\n",
              name, ever, peak, peak_month))
}
```

## What to notice

**Correcting the record late barely reduces how many people ever believed it.** In the late-evidence world, almost everyone has already passed through the believing state before the papers appear. The correction changes what people believe *now*; it cannot change what they believed for three years, or the decisions they made meanwhile — the shoppers who stopped buying quinoa out of conscience, and whose purchases, on the evidence in the article, were helping the people they were worried about.

**Timing beats content.** This model has no term at all for how *convincing* the evidence is. It does not need one. The arrival date alone drives most of the difference. That is an uncomfortable result for anyone who believes better arguments win, and it is why "rapid response" and pre-registered data infrastructure are treated as serious epistemic institutions rather than public relations.

**The debunking never fully wins.** Notice that the pale grey "never heard it" band never disappears, and believers linger. In this model, as in reality, some people simply never encounter the correction. Retractions travel through a smaller network than the original claim.

**A caveat you should always attach to this model.** The epidemic analogy imports assumptions that may not hold for ideas: that everyone mixes with everyone, that believing is a single binary state, that hearing the correction is like recovering from an illness. Real beliefs are held in networks, with degrees of conviction, and with motivated resistance. The right response is not to abandon the model but to know which of its conclusions depend on the shaky assumptions. Here, "late corrections are weak" is robust across almost any variant. Specific percentages are not.

## Exercises

1. Find, by trial and error, the latest month at which the correction still keeps the eventual believer share under half. Is that a realistic timescale for academic publication? What would it take to hit it?
2. Set `EVIDENCE_EFFECT = 30`, making the debunking overwhelmingly persuasive, and keep it late. Compare to an early but weak correction (`evidence_month=12`, `EVIDENCE_EFFECT=2`). Which does better? What does that imply about where to invest?
3. **The hard one.** This model treats the true and false claims symmetrically — both are just claims that spread. Is there anything in the structure that would make truth spread better? If not, what does that suggest about relying on the marketplace of ideas?

---
# Coda — Two different things called "models"

Everything above is a **mechanistic** model: we specified how we think the world works, and derived what would follow. But the papers the article reports do something else entirely. Bellemare, Gitter and Fajardo-Gonzalez cleaned ten years of ENAHO data covering the boom and the years before it, split households into three groups — those who grow and eat quinoa, those who eat but do not grow it, and those who do neither — and compared how each group's welfare moved as the price rose. That is a **statistical** model. It does not say why anything happens. It asks whether a pattern in observed data could plausibly have arisen by chance.

Both are called models. They answer different questions and they fail in different ways. A mechanistic model can be beautifully coherent and describe no world that exists. A statistical model can be perfectly estimated and mean nothing, because a difference between groups is not automatically an effect.

The specific difficulty in this case is one the article steps around in a single sentence: quinoa eaters who do not grow it are roughly twice as well off as growers. So if you simply compared growers and non-growers *after* the boom, growers would look worse off — not because the boom hurt them but because they were poorer to begin with. The comparison you want is not between groups but between *changes* in groups. Below is a small simulation of that idea, called **difference-in-differences**, which is the workhorse of applied social science.

We generate fake households where we *know* the true answer, and then check whether the method recovers it. That is the only situation in which you can ever validate a statistical method, and it is why simulation belongs in a methods course.

```{r coda-did, fig.width=7.6, fig.height=4.9, out.width="100%"}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CODA: why you compare changes, not levels
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

N <- 4000                     # households in our synthetic survey
TRUE_EFFECT <- 500.0          # the real gain to growers from the boom, in soles.
                              # We KNOW this because we are about to create it.

# Half the households grow quinoa. Growers are poorer to start with - this is the
# fact from the article that makes naive comparison misleading.
is_grower <- runif(N) < 0.5
baseline_welfare <- ifelse(is_grower, 4800.0, 9600.0)

# Everyone's welfare rises over the period, because Peru grew. The article is
# explicit that all three groups saw living standards improve.
COMMON_TREND <- 900.0

# Survey noise: every household is idiosyncratic, and surveys are imperfect.
noise_before <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 1200)
noise_after  <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 1200)

welfare_before <- baseline_welfare + noise_before
welfare_after  <- baseline_welfare + COMMON_TREND + TRUE_EFFECT * is_grower + noise_after

# --- The wrong comparison: growers vs non-growers, after the boom only -------
# The "!" means "not", so !is_grower picks out the non-growers.
naive <- mean(welfare_after[is_grower]) - mean(welfare_after[!is_grower])

# --- The right comparison: how much each group CHANGED -----------------------
change_growers     <- mean(welfare_after[is_grower])  - mean(welfare_before[is_grower])
change_non_growers <- mean(welfare_after[!is_grower]) - mean(welfare_before[!is_grower])
did <- change_growers - change_non_growers     # difference in the differences

cat(sprintf("True effect of the boom on growers      : %+8.0f soles\n", TRUE_EFFECT))
cat(strrep("-", 58), "\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("Naive comparison of levels after the boom: %+8.0f soles  <-- badly wrong, wrong sign\n", naive))
cat(sprintf("Change among growers                     : %+8.0f soles\n", change_growers))
cat(sprintf("Change among non-growers                 : %+8.0f soles\n", change_non_growers))
cat(sprintf("Difference-in-differences estimate       : %+8.0f soles  <-- close to the truth\n", did))

# --- Picture it --------------------------------------------------------------
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(4.5, 5, 3.5, 6))

grower_line     <- c(mean(welfare_before[is_grower]),  mean(welfare_after[is_grower]))
non_grower_line <- c(mean(welfare_before[!is_grower]), mean(welfare_after[!is_grower]))

# The dashed line shows where growers WOULD have ended up with only the common
# trend and no boom effect. The gap between it and reality is the estimate.
counterfactual <- mean(welfare_before[is_grower]) + change_non_growers

plot(c(0, 1), range(c(grower_line, non_grower_line)) + c(-500, 500), type = "n",
     xlim = c(-0.15, 1.35), xaxt = "n", xlab = "",
     ylab = "average welfare (soles)",
     main = "Coda: growers stay poorer in levels, yet gain more")
axis(1, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("before the boom", "after the boom"))
add_grid()

lines(c(0, 1), grower_line,     lwd = 2.5, col = TAB["blue"])
points(c(0, 1), grower_line,    pch = 19, col = TAB["blue"])
lines(c(0, 1), non_grower_line, lwd = 2.5, col = TAB["orange"])
points(c(0, 1), non_grower_line, pch = 19, col = TAB["orange"])

lines(c(0, 1), c(mean(welfare_before[is_grower]), counterfactual),
      lty = 2, lwd = 1.5, col = TAB["grey"])

# A double-headed arrow (code = 3) marking the gap that the method estimates.
arrows(1, counterfactual, 1, grower_line[2], code = 3, length = 0.07,
       lwd = 1.8, col = TAB["red"])
text(1.03, (grower_line[2] + counterfactual) / 2, "this gap is\nthe estimate",
     col = TAB["red"], cex = 0.8, adj = 0)

legend("left", legend = c("quinoa growers (poorer, gain more)",
                          "non-growers (richer, gain less)",
                          "growers' counterfactual path"),
       col = c(TAB["blue"], TAB["orange"], TAB["grey"]),
       lwd = c(2.5, 2.5, 1.5), lty = c(1, 1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
```

## What to notice

**Levels and changes can point in opposite directions.** The naive comparison says growers are far worse off; the correct one says the boom helped them. Both statements about the data are true. Only one of them answers the question asked. Most bad quantitative social science is not arithmetic error — it is a well-computed answer to a question nobody asked.

**The dashed line is doing all the work.** Difference-in-differences rests on an assumption you cannot observe: that without the boom, growers' welfare would have moved *parallel* to non-growers'. If Andean agriculture was on a different trajectory for unrelated reasons — weather, roads, migration — the estimate is wrong and nothing in the data will tell you so. Every credible study of this type spends most of its length defending that assumption.

**"It is a beast to work with."** Bellemare's remark about ENAHO deserves its place in a methods course. Someone — Johanna Fajardo-Gonzalez, named in the article — spent months cleaning ten years of survey data before any of this could be estimated. That labour is invisible in the published result and is usually the difference between a real finding and a spurious one.

---

# Closing synthesis: what the seven models add up to

| # | Model | Type | The idea it teaches |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Net-seller welfare | Static accounting | A model with no computation can overturn a headline |
| 2 | Cobweb | Deterministic dynamics | Delay plus negative feedback produces oscillation |
| 3 | Logistic diffusion | Coupled dynamics | Equifinality: one pattern, many possible mechanisms |
| 4 | Soil and herds | Stock and flow | Stocks have memory; good years can hide a drawdown |
| 5 | Diversity game | Strategic interaction | Individually rational, collectively bad |
| 6 | Demand with a floor | Calibration and fit | A model that cannot fit is a model with content |
| 7 | Spread of a claim | Contagion | Timing can dominate truth |
| — | Difference-in-differences | Statistical inference | Compare changes, not levels |

Four things to take from putting them side by side.

**No model is the model.** Seven models of one article, all defensible, several mutually inconsistent about mechanism. A model is not a small copy of the world; it is an instrument for asking one question at a time. Choosing which question is the researcher's job, and no algorithm does it for you.

**Simple models earn their keep by being wrong in visible places.** Model 1 is almost embarrassingly crude and it settles the central dispute. Model 6 fails and the failure locates a real mechanism. A large simulation with forty parameters fitted to the same data would have told you less, because when everything can be adjusted, nothing is tested.

**Time horizon is a modeling choice with moral weight.** Models 1 and 4 do not disagree about facts. They disagree about when to stop counting. "Was the quinoa boom good?" cannot be answered without saying good *by when*, and that is not something the data decides.

**Mechanism and measurement need each other.** The mechanistic models above generate hypotheses but cannot say what happened. The statistical work in the papers establishes what happened but not why. Computational social science, done well, is the practice of holding both and refusing to let either off the hook.

---

## Suggested assignment

Pick any *one* sentence from the article that we did not model. Then:

1. State the causal claim inside it in one sentence.
2. Write the smallest model that could be wrong about it — no more than about fifteen lines of code.
3. Identify the one parameter your conclusion is most sensitive to, and say honestly how you would go about measuring it.
4. Name one fact that your model cannot accommodate, and say what you would build next.

Step 4 is worth the most marks.
